w: Launched in 1860, Warrior and her sister Black Prince were the first iron-hulled, armour-plated warships afloat, Britain's answer to France's ironclad Gloire. She never fired a shot in anger, served as an oil jetty from 1927, and returned to Portsmouth in 1987 after an eight-year restoration.
s: The ironclad that made every other warship obsolete
_facts: Built 1859-61, a response to France's ironclad Gloire
First iron-hulled, armour-plated warship afloat
Served as an oil jetty 1927-1979 before restoration
Returned to Portsmouth as a museum ship in 1987

w: Built on the ruins of Haselworth Castle to guard Portsmouth Harbour during the American War of Independence, Fort Monckton was rebuilt in the 1880s as a Palmerston fort. It now trains Britain's intelligence services, its 18th-century footprint on the Gosport shore still intact.
s: An 18th-century fort now training the intelligence services
_facts: Built on the ruins of Haselworth Castle at the start of the American War of Independence
Rebuilt in the 1880s as a Palmerston fort
Now a training centre for the intelligence services

w: The Royal Navy's first submarine, launched in 1901, Holland 1 sank in 1913 while under tow to the scrapyard after decommissioning. Recovered from the seabed in 1982, she went on display at the Royal Navy Submarine Museum in Gosport - and her original battery bank, once cleaned and recharged, was found to still work.
s: Britain's first submarine, sunk, salvaged, still wired
_facts: First submarine commissioned by the Royal Navy, launched 1901
Sank in 1913 while under tow for scrapping
Recovered in 1982, now on display at the Royal Navy Submarine Museum
Original battery bank still functional after cleaning

w: One of four Palmerston sea forts built in the Solent against a feared French invasion, Horse Sand Fort rises 200 feet across the water, built 1865-1880 with two floors, a basement, and armour plating on every side. It still stands offshore, one of Portsmouth's odder silhouettes.
s: A Victorian invasion-fear fort marooned in the Solent
_facts: One of four Palmerston sea forts in the Solent off Portsmouth
200 feet across, built 1865-1880
Two floors and a basement, armour-plated all round

w: Built in 1915, this M29-class monitor fought at Gallipoli and later in Russia during the 1919 Allied intervention, before decades as a minelayer trainer and floating office under other names. She is one of only three Royal Navy WWI warships still afloat, and the only surviving Allied ship from Gallipoli.
s: A WWI gunboat that outlived every name it was given
_facts: M29-class monitor built 1915
Served at Gallipoli and in the 1919 Allied intervention in Russia
One of only three surviving Royal Navy WWI warships
Only surviving Allied ship from the Gallipoli campaign

w: Built up over five centuries, from a 1431 blockhouse to Cold War submarine base structures added in the mid-1960s, Fort Blockhouse commands the best view of the entrance to Portsmouth Harbour. As HMS Dolphin it was home to the Royal Navy Submarine Service for most of the 20th century, until the boats left in the 1990s.
s: Five centuries of fort-building at the harbour mouth
_facts: Built in stages from 1431 to the mid-1960s
Home of the Royal Navy Submarine Service as HMS Dolphin
Best view of the entrance to Portsmouth Harbour
Submarines left in the 1990s

n: Cathedral of St John the Evangelist
w: Dedicated in 1882, this Roman Catholic cathedral is the seat of the Bishop of Portsmouth, mother church of a diocese spanning Hampshire, Berkshire and the Channel Islands. It shares the city with a second cathedral, the Anglican St Thomas's, about a mile south - one of few English cities with two.
s: One of two cathedrals sharing a single small city
_facts: Dedicated 10 August 1882
Seat of the Bishop of Portsmouth (Roman Catholic)
Diocese covers Hampshire, Berkshire and the Channel Islands
One of two cathedrals in Portsmouth

w: Henry VIII's flagship carrack sank off Spithead in 1545 leading an attack on a French invasion fleet, and lay on the seabed until divers found her in 1971. Raising her in 1982 was one of the most complex maritime salvage operations ever attempted - the wreck, with thousands of Tudor artefacts, has been on display at the dockyard since.
s: Henry VIII's warship, sunk in battle, raised centuries on
_facts: Launched 1511, served 34 years, sank 19 July 1545 off Spithead
Wreck located 1971, raised 11 October 1982
One of the most complex and expensive maritime salvage projects in history
Thousands of recovered Tudor-period artefacts on display

w: For centuries this was HM Dockyard, Portsmouth, once the largest industrial site in the world and now one of three Royal Navy operating bases. Downsized in 1984 and partly privatised in 1998, it still homes two-thirds of the Royal Navy's surface fleet, including carriers HMS Queen Elizabeth and Prince of Wales.
s: Once the world's biggest industrial site, still working
_facts: Formerly HM Dockyard, Portsmouth; once the world's largest industrial site
One of three Royal Navy operating bases, with Clyde and Devonport
Downsized and renamed Fleet Maintenance and Repair Organisation in 1984
Home to two-thirds of the Royal Navy's surface fleet, including two carriers

w: Portsmouth residents chose this 170-metre design in a 1998 public poll, and it opened in 2005 shaped like a billowing sail, a nod to the city's maritime past. Three stacked viewing platforms sit at 100, 105 and 110 metres up; it has carried Emirates branding and, since 2023, Macmillan Cancer Support sponsorship.
s: The sail-shaped tower Portsmouth voted into being
_facts: 170 metres tall, opened 18 October 2005
Design chosen by public poll of Portsmouth residents in 1998
Three viewing platforms at 100m, 105m and 110m
Named after a spinnaker sail

w: A Norman keep rises inside the walls of a Roman Saxon Shore fort here, a rare double layer of fortification at the head of Portsmouth Harbour. King John used it as a hunting lodge, the French captured it in 1216, and a plot against Henry V uncovered here was later dramatised in Shakespeare's play.
s: A Norman castle built inside an old Roman fort
_facts: Norman keep built within the Roman Saxon Shore fort of Portus Adurni
Favoured hunting lodge of King John
Besieged and captured by the French in 1216
Plot against Henry V uncovered here, dramatised in Shakespeare's Henry V

w: The Cathedral Church of St Thomas of Canterbury has stood at the centre of Old Portsmouth since the medieval period, but only became a cathedral in 1935 when the Diocese of Portsmouth was formed. It is one of two cathedrals in the city - the Roman Catholic St John's sits about a mile to the north.
s: A medieval church that waited centuries for cathedral status
_facts: Anglican cathedral, seat of the Bishop of Portsmouth since 1935
Located in the centre of Old Portsmouth
One of two cathedrals in the city

w: Henry VIII built this artillery fort on Portsea Island in 1544 against invasion from France, and a Tudor engraving shows him visiting during the 1545 Battle of the Solent, when the Mary Rose sank nearby. Parliamentary forces stormed it in 1642, and it was reinforced again in 1814 and the 1850s-60s.
s: The fort Henry VIII visited the day the Mary Rose sank
_facts: Built by Henry VIII in 1544, part of the King's Device programme
Cowdray engraving depicts Henry VIII visiting during the 1545 Battle of the Solent
Stormed by Parliamentary forces in 1642
Reinforced in 1814 and the 1850s-60s

w: Built during the Napoleonic Wars to mass-produce pulley blocks for the Royal Navy, the Block Mills used all-metal machine tools chiefly designed by Marc Isambard Brunel, starting the age of mass production - a seminal Industrial Revolution site that also housed the Admiralty's first stationary steam engines.
s: Where the Industrial Revolution's mass production began
_facts: Built during the Napoleonic Wars to supply pulley blocks
Machine tools chiefly designed by Marc Isambard Brunel
Started the age of mass production using all-metal machine tools
Site of the Admiralty's first stationary steam engines

w: Built in 1890 as Portsmouth Town Hall, this landmark was gutted by Second World War bombing and largely rebuilt in the 1950s by architect Ernest Berry Webber. It now hosts concerts, weddings and conferences from a pedestrianised square next to Portsmouth and Southsea station, and carries Grade II listed status.
s: The town hall the Blitz gutted and the Fifties rebuilt
_facts: Built 1890 as Portsmouth Town Hall; renamed Guildhall in 1926
Heavily damaged by WWII bombing
Rebuilt in the 1950s by Ernest Berry Webber
Grade II listed

w: Dedicated to the Royal Marines since their founding in 1664, this museum became part of the National Museum of the Royal Navy in 2011. Its galleries at the old Eastney Barracks have been closed since 2017, awaiting relocation to Portsmouth Historic Dockyard - worth checking status before visiting.
s: The Marines' museum, packed up and awaiting a new home
_facts: Covers Royal Marines history from 1664 to the present
Became part of the National Museum of the Royal Navy in 2011
Galleries at Eastney Barracks closed since 2017 pending relocation to the Historic Dockyard
